name: Dermastamping with minoxidil

lead: Dermastamping is a microneedling variant in which a needled stamp is used on the scalp before topical minoxidil. Users say it improves absorption and stimulates follicles.
A small pilot study cited by Wikipedia found the combination more effective than minoxidil alone in androgenetic alopecia, but evidence is limited.

paras: Microneedling creates tiny skin punctures, proposed to enhance drug delivery and trigger wound-healing growth factors. Minoxidil is converted to minoxidil sulfate and affects potassium channels and the follicle cycle.
Risks include skin irritation, shedding, and infection with poor hygiene; health agencies have warned of blood-borne infection risks from microneedling in non-medical settings.

lead: Dermastamping with minoxidil is a hair-loss routine in which a person uses a microneedle stamping device on the scalp and applies topical minoxidil afterwards, on the idea that small skin punctures improve absorption or stimulate follicles. It is a variant of dermarolling.[1]

Encyclopedic sources report that some studies found microneedling combined with minoxidil more effective than minoxidil alone, citing a small pilot study of androgenetic alopecia.[1] A 2024 retrospective study of 230 people with alopecia areata examined microneedle application of minoxidil with triamcinolone, a different condition.[2]
Safety concerns for microneedling are greatest in non-medical settings without infection control.[1]

paras: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy or dermarolling, involves repeatedly puncturing skin with tiny needles.[1] Stamp devices are a form of this approach. Topical minoxidil is applied to treat pattern hair loss; sources describe its mechanism as incompletely understood, with effects on blood vessels, growth factors and the follicle cycle proposed.[3]
Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn as an oral blood pressure drug, and topical minoxidil (Rogaine) was approved in the US for male baldness in 1988 and became available over the counter in 1996.[3]

A 2024 retrospective study of 230 patients with alopecia areata compared microneedle treatment with minoxidil plus triamcinolone with a control group; this concerned a different type of hair loss.[2] A registered trial (NCT06218394) compares microneedling with autologous growth factor in female androgenetic alopecia, with an unknown status.[4]
Encyclopedia summaries note that microneedling with minoxidil outperformed minoxidil alone in a small pilot study of androgenetic alopecia.[1]

Microneedling in non-medical settings by people untrained in infection control carries risk of spreading blood-borne infections, according to a New Mexico health department statement; in 2024 the CDC reported three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at a spa.[1] Topical minoxidil commonly causes scalp irritation, and temporary shedding is a listed effect.[3] Absorption through microneedled skin has not been characterised in the sources reviewed.

Small studies suggest microneedling combined with minoxidil may be more effective than minoxidil alone in androgenetic alopecia, according to a pilot study cited by Wikipedia.[1] A 2024 retrospective study examined microneedle minoxidil with triamcinolone in alopecia areata.[2] A registered trial of microneedling in female androgenetic alopecia is listed with unknown status.[4]

lore.intro: Dermastamping appears in hair-loss communities as a way to raise results from minoxidil.
